title: Variables
summary: Naming values with let and const, changing them, and the two empty values undefined and null.

misconceptions.description: Believes a variable declared without a value holds 0, empty text or causes an error, instead of holding undefined.
Mixes up names and text: believes console.log prints the variable's name, or that quotes around a name still read the variable.
Reads the value of a neighbouring variable instead of the one a line or question is about.
Believes a variable that was made from another variable keeps following it, so later changes to the source also change the result.
Reads the value from a different moment than the one asked about, such as the first value or the final result.
Believes assigning a new value adds it to the old one instead of replacing it.
Believes assigning to a const name works, or is skipped quietly, instead of stopping the program with an error.
Believes const causes the wrong kind of error or an error in the wrong place, such as on any use of the name or on any variable.
Expects typeof to answer null for the value null.
Treats undefined and null as the same value, or as the same type.

conceptCard.title: Naming a value with let
conceptCard.body: let creates a variable, a name that holds a value. Write let, a name, = and the value. Use the name without quotes to read the value. Quotes make plain text instead. A let with no value holds undefined until you store one.

conceptCard.title: Changing what a variable holds
conceptCard.body: A variable can hold a new value later. Write its name, = and the new value, without let. The old value is gone. The right side is worked out first, so cups = cups + 3 uses the old value. A copy of a variable gets the value only, not a link.

conceptCard.title: Fixed names with const
conceptCard.body: const makes a name that cannot get a new value. You give the value where you declare it. Assigning to it later stops the program with a TypeError. Use const for values that stay fixed and let for values that change.

conceptCard.title: undefined and null
conceptCard.body: undefined means no value was stored yet. null is a value you store on purpose to say empty. typeof answers undefined for the first and object for null, a quirk of the language that was never fixed.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

A new variable does not start at zero. Zero is a number, and nothing was stored here.
The name was declared on line 1, so JavaScript knows it. A declared name with no value can be read without an error.

items.prompt: What value does total hold right after line 3 has run?

options.feedback: Right. Line 3 multiplies the two stored values, 6 and 2, and stores the result in total.
That is the value of left, which line 4 stores later. The question stops after line 3.
That is eggs. Line 3 stores a new value in total, found by multiplying eggs by cartons.

items.explanation: Line 3 reads eggs and cartons, multiplies 6 by 2 and stores 12 in total. Line 4 uses that 12 later to make left.
hints: Follow the lines in order and stop after line 3.
Each line stores a value in the name on its left.
Multiply the values of the two names on line 3.

items.prompt: Fill the blank with the variable that holds the booked seats, so the program prints 18.

options.feedback: Right. It holds 12, and 30 - 12 is 18.
This subtracts the seats from themselves, so the program prints 0.
No variable called free was declared, so the program stops with a ReferenceError.

items.explanation: The program must subtract the booked seats from 30. The variable booked, declared on line 2, holds 12, and 30 - 12 gives 18.
hints: Look at line 2 to see which name holds the number of taken seats.
Only names that were declared can be used.
Subtract something from 30 to get 18: work out what that something is, then find the name that holds it.

items.prompt: Which statement explains the two lines this program prints?

options.text: Without quotes, mood reads the stored value. With quotes, it is only the text mood.
options.feedback: Right. The first line prints calm and the second prints the word mood.

options.text: Both lines print calm, because quotes do not change what a name means.
options.feedback: Quotes turn the letters into plain text. They are no longer a name, so the stored value is not read.

options.text: Both lines print mood, because console.log shows the name of a variable.
options.feedback: console.log shows values, not names. The unquoted mood is replaced by the value stored under it.

items.explanation: An unquoted name is read as the variable and gives its stored value, calm. Text in quotes is just text, so line 3 prints the word mood.
hints: Compare line 2 with line 3.
Quotes make plain text instead of a name.
One line reads the variable. The other line does not.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

You expected area to follow width. A variable stores a result, not the rule that made it.

items.prompt: What value does baked hold right after line 3 has run?

options.feedback: Right. Line 2 copied the value 24. Changing the copy does not touch baked.
You treated the two names as one box. Line 2 copied the value, so the names are independent.
That is the number taken away on line 3. The question asks about baked, which never had 15 stored.

items.explanation: Line 2 copies the number 24 into onShelf. Line 3 then replaces the value in onShelf only. The name baked still holds 24.
hints: Ask which name line 3 changes.
Copying a variable copies its value, not a link.
Line 3 changes onShelf. It never touches baked.

items.prompt: Fill the blank so line 2 takes 2 away from spaces and the program prints 28.

options.feedback: Right. Line 2 works out 30 - 2 using the old value and stores 28.
This adds 2 to the old value, so the program prints 32.
This multiplies the old value by 2, so the program prints 60.
This divides the old value by 2, so the program prints 15.

items.explanation: Line 2 works out the right side first, using the old value 30, and stores the result in spaces. Only 30 - 2 gives 28, so the old value is replaced by 28.
hints: Look at line 2: the new value is worked out from the old spaces.
The right side of = is worked out first, using the old value.
Try each chip on 30 and 2 and keep the one that gives 28.

items.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints 27.
items.explanation: Declare first and print last. Doubling 12 gives 24, and adding 3 gives 27. Adding 3 first would give 15 and then 30.

Try the doubling line before the adding line.

items.prompt: A variable starts as start. Then it is set to itself plus deposit, then to itself minus fee. Write an expression for its final value.
items.explanation: Each reassignment starts from the value the variable holds at that moment. The first adds deposit to start. The second subtracts fee from that result.
hints: Write the steps one after the other.
Every step uses the value left by the step before.
Start with start, add deposit, then take away fee.

Reading a const is allowed. Assigning to it again is not.

items.prompt: What does this code print?

typeof never answers null. For the value null it gives a different word, an old quirk of the language.
The two values are not the same. One is a variable with nothing stored, and it has its own type name.

items.explanation: An unfilled variable has type undefined. For null, typeof answers object, a quirk kept for old code. console.log prints both words with a space.

items.prompt: driver holds a name or null. Write an expression that gives Driver: and a space, then the value of driver. For null it gives Driver: null.
items.explanation: null is a real value, and joined to text with + it becomes the word null. So the label and driver join into Driver: null. typeof would give the type name object instead of the value.
hints: You need the value of driver itself, not its type.
The + sign joins texts, and a null joined to text shows as the word null.
Put the label first, with the space after its colon, then driver.
